required_items.text: Written policies and procedures governing 24-hour availability to licensed professional nursing staff by active patients receiving skilled care. They must describe an on-call system in which designated nursing staff can communicate directly with the patient. (Skilled agencies only.)

A home health agency that does not provide skilled services shall have written policies and procedures that address the availability of a registered nurse supervisor during hours of patient service. (This applies to a non-skilled personal care agency.)

If the agency operates a satellite office, it must: (a) ensure coverage of professional staff based on projected clients; (b) coordinate care and services by staff; (c) ensure supervision and service provision when staff are absent; (d) maintain communication and integration of services between main and satellite offices; (e) provide access to patient records at the satellite office; (f) monitor daily clinical and administrative activities, services, personnel and administrative issues; (g) ensure periodic onsite visits by the administrator; (h) make the satellite office's hours available to the public if they differ from the main office. (Conditional on having a satellite office.)

Written designation of an on-site alternate administrator for the administrator's absences. This person has responsibility and authority for daily operation during those absences and must meet ss. 400.462(1) and 400.476(1), F.S.
The director of nursing must maintain and adhere to agency procedure and patient care policy manuals. (Not required for an agency that does not provide skilled care; see (2)(i).)

The director of nursing, administrator or alternate administrator shall establish policies and procedures on biomedical waste for agencies providing nursing and physical therapy services. (Applies only if those services are provided.)
Policies and procedures consistent with recommended CDC and OSHA guidelines for safety, universal precautions and infection control procedures.
Set or adopt policies for, and keep records of, criteria for admission to service, case assignments and case management.
Establish and adopt policies and procedures for the delegation process of nursing tasks and activities as specified in Chapter 64B9-14, F.A.C.

A process to verify that skilled nursing and personal care services were provided. The director of nursing must be able to produce a certified report of home health services provided by a named direct-service or contracted staff person for a specified period. The report is due to a surveyor within two hours of the request, or within three hours if the period requested is longer than one year.

An ongoing quality assurance program with at least quarterly documented review of a sample of active and closed clinical records. It must assure that: 1. the agency accepts patients whose service needs it can meet; 2. case assignment and management are appropriate, adequate and consistent with the plan of care, and plans of care are individualized; 3. nursing and other services are coordinated, appropriate, adequate and consistent with plans of care; 4. all services and outcomes are completely and legibly documented, dated and signed in the clinical record; 5. the agency's policies and procedures are followed; 6. confidentiality of patient data is maintained; 7. QA findings are used to improve services.

RN assignment of personal care tasks to LPNs, CNAs and home health aides. The RN maintains full responsibility for those tasks and must ensure the aide or CNA is qualified for each assignment based on training and experience.

RN supervisory visits of unlicensed assistive personnel under s. 400.487(3), F.S., with written consent from the patient or the patient's guardian or legal representative for the RN to enter the home. The RN provides on-site supervision as needed, based on the severity of the patient's condition and the aide's or CNA's training and experience. Supervisory visits are documented in patient files.
Provision in agency policies and procedures for annual evaluation of the LPN's performance of duties by the registered nurse. (Applies if LPNs are used.)

Before a CNA works, documentation of current Florida CNA certification (or a current out-of-state certificate). Before a home health aide works, documentation of at least 40 hours of training or a passed competency test. Training subjects: 1. communication skills; 2. observation, reporting and documentation; 3. reading and recording temperature, pulse and respiration; 4. basic infection control; 5. basic body functions to be reported to the RN supervisor; 6. maintenance of a clean and safe environment; 7. recognition of emergencies and follow-up; 8. physical, emotional and developmental characteristics of populations served, including respect for the patient or client, privacy and property; 9. personal hygiene and grooming techniques; 10. safe transfer techniques and ambulation; 11. normal range of motion and positioning; 12. nutrition and fluid intake; 13. cultural differences in families; 14. food preparation and household chores; 15. assistance with self-administered medication (minimum 2 hours of training, including verification that the aide can read the prescription label); 16. other pertinent topics.

Home health aide training must be performed by or under the general supervision of an RN with at least two years of nursing experience, one of them in home health care. An agency may instead administer the Home Health Aide Competency Test (AHCA 3110-1007) and must keep documentation of the aide's passing result. The practical portion must be administered and evaluated by an RN, or by an LPN under RN supervision.
Home health aides and CNAs must receive in-service training each calendar year and maintain current CPR certification from an approved provider.

Home health aide and CNA responsibilities include: 1. personal care activities in a written assignment by a licensed health professional; 2. maintenance of a clean, safe and healthy environment; 3. other activities taught by a licensed professional for a specific patient, limited to the listed tasks (a–l); 4. keeping records of personal health care activities; 5. observing and reporting appearance and gross behavioral changes to the RN; 6. supervision of self-administered medication, limited to the four listed steps.

Self-administered medication assistance: an RN review and reconciliation of all prescribed and over-the-counter medications, to confirm the patient is medically stable with routine scheduled medications. A licensed health care professional must inform the patient or caregiver of the arrangement and obtain written consent under s. 400.488(2), F.S. Permitted aide actions are listed in (5)(o)1-4.

Responsibilities the home health aide and CNA may not perform (the list starts at 1. therapeutic services requiring licensure and runs through at least 10). The fetched page was cut off partway through this list, so retrieve the full text from the rule.

Each home health agency shall have written policies and procedures that delineate the agency's position with respect to state law and rules on advance directives. The policies shall not condition treatment or admission on whether the individual has executed or waived an advance directive. Conflicts between the agency's policies and a patient's advance directive are handled under Chapter 765, F.S.

The advance-directive policy must include giving each adult patient, before services begin, a copy of 'Health Care Advance Directives – The Patients' Right to Decide' (AHCA, rev. April 2006) or an equivalent written description of Florida law.
The advance-directive policy must include giving each adult patient, before services begin, written information about the agency's policies respecting advance directives.

The advance-directive policy must include the requirement that the patient's medical record document whether or not an advance directive has been executed. A copy of any executed directive goes in the record. If no copy is received, the agency documents that it requested one.
DNRO: cardiopulmonary resuscitation may be withheld or withdrawn only if a valid Do Not Resuscitate Order is present, executed under s. 401.45, F.S. (Department of Health form; rule 64J-2.018).

Acceptance of patients or clients: there must be a reasonable expectation that services can be provided safely in the patient's residence. This includes the ability to communicate with the patient (or the patient's designee) through a same-language staff person or interpreter, or through translation technology. The agency must assure the patient receives services as defined in the plan of care or written agreement, including all assigned visits.

At the start of services, a written agreement between the agency and the patient, client or legal representative, including the information in s. 400.487(1), F.S. It must be signed and dated by an agency representative and the patient, client or representative. A copy goes to the patient or client and the original goes in the file.

For homemaker/companion clients and for home health aide clients who do not need a practitioner's treatment order, the written agreement serves as the service provision plan under s. 400.491(2), F.S. It is kept for one year after services end.

Termination of services for patients or clients needing continuing care: develop a plan and make a referral to another agency or provider before termination. Give written notice of the termination date, the reason (s. 400.491, F.S.) and the plan for continued services. This does not apply to patients paying privately who default through non-payment. The agency should provide social work assistance to help determine eligibility for government-funded programs.

A written comprehensive emergency management plan, prepared and maintained under s. 400.492, F.S., following the criteria in the CEMP (AHCA Form 3110-1022, Rev. March 2013), which is used as the plan format. The plan describes how the agency establishes and maintains an effective response to emergencies and disasters.
The completed plan is forwarded electronically for approval to the contact designated by the Department of Health. The agency reviews the plan annually and makes substantive changes.

Changes in telephone numbers of staff coordinating emergency response (including after-hours numbers) must be reported to the county Emergency Management office and the county health department. A new owner reviews the plan after a change of ownership.

In an emergency, all staff designated for emergency measures must be informed of their duties. If telephone service is unavailable, the agency must have a communication contingency plan (for example cell phones, ham radio, public announcements, driving to the home, or contacting police or rescue services).

On admission, inform patients and caregivers of the county special needs registry (s. 252.355, F.S.). Document in the patient file whether the patient will evacuate or stay, whether the caregiver can take over services, and whether the agency must continue services. For ALF or adult family care home residents, find out the facility's evacuation plan and document it.

On imminent threat of an emergency, contact patients needing ongoing services (and the ALFs and adult family care homes served) to confirm each patient's plan. Before an emergency, establish procedures stating to what extent the agency will continue care during and after it. Ascertain which patients staying home need agency care, and designate staff to continue services.

If the agency ceases operation during an emergency, it must inform affected patients, notify the ALFs and adult family care homes served, and make arrangements for nursing personnel to continue essential services. It must report its status to the local emergency operations center. When unable to continue services to special needs patients, the record must document the efforts made to comply with the plan.

Collect registration information for special needs patients who need continuing care in a disaster and submit it to the county Emergency Management office. Educate registered patients that special needs shelters are an option of last resort and that services may not equal those received at home.

Maintain a current prioritized patient list with the information in s. 400.492(2), F.S., and furnish it to the county health department and Emergency Management office on request. The record of each special needs patient must include the s. 400.492(1) information. The agency must keep in the special needs patient's home a list of patient-specific medications, supplies and equipment (names, dose, frequency, route, time, allergies, physician, pharmacy).

Homemaker/companion registration: the application must state the specific geographic area to be served. Providers holding a registration as of July 1, 2015 may keep serving the counties listed on it if a plan for supervision of staff working outside the primary geographic service area is documented.

Confidential client record (homemaker/companion providers): (a) client's full legal name, address, phone, age, and disability if it is the basis for service; (b) name and phone of the emergency contact, next of kin or legal guardian, and physician; (c) copy of any contract or written service agreement; (d) services provided, with duration and frequency of visits; (e) dietary restrictions, if the provider prepares, orders or accompanies the client to meals; (f) food allergies; (g) activity limitations pertaining to service delivery; (h) copy of any written termination notice.

On accepting a client, there must be a reasonable expectation that the requested services can be provided adequately and safely in the residence. The provider must obtain all needed service-delivery information and supply employees or independent contractors capable of delivering the contracted services, including all visits.

notes: I did not find a single AHCA policy checklist or plan-of-operation form for Florida personal care. The required_items list is therefore built from the Chapter 59A-8, F.A.C. sections that require written policies, plans or procedures. Item numbering follows the rule text. Florida licenses the agency on AHCA Form 3110-1011 (HHA) or Form 3110-1003 (homemaker/companion), and AHCA surveys compliance. The survey tool is AHCA's ASPEN 'Home Health Agencies' regulation set, which I located but did not review. The CEMP (AHCA Form 3110-1022) is the mandated format for the emergency plan, and DOH reviews it. Items marked conditional apply only to skilled agencies, to agencies that provide nursing or PT services, or to agencies with satellite offices or LPNs. A non-skilled agency is not required to have a director of nursing under 59A-8.0095(2)(i). A reviewer would expect one organized policy manual, plus the CEMP, the aide training and competency documentation, a sample service agreement, and a sample client record. A non-skilled agency must show RN supervision arrangements and RN supervisory visits. Not reviewed or fetched (check before relying on this list): 59A-8.0215 (Plan of Care), 59A-8.0216 (RN delegation), 59A-8.0219 (medication administration), 59A-8.022 (clinical records), s. 400.487 and s. 400.491 F.S., s. 400.509 F.S., s. 400.4785/430.5025 F.S. dementia training, and the licensure application and addendum forms. The Cornell LII copies are unofficial, and the official text is on flrules.org (Florida Administrative Code). Excluded as application paperwork: forms, fees, financials, background screening and insurance.
